title: The Outpatient Room and the New Revelation: the doctor who invented deduction and spent his fortune on the dead
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Edinburgh House and the Jesuit Years

stops.name: 11 Picardy Place, Edinburgh: the birth
stops.date_confidence: Date and address attested: Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', gives the birth verbatim as 22 May 1859 at 11 Picardy Place, Edinburgh. The coordinate is the weak point. Three research lenses returned three different points for the same address (55.9581/-3.1875, 55.9578/-3.1882, 55.9578/-3.1873) and no coordinate source for Picardy Place could be fetched, since Wikipedia has no article for the street. 55.9578/-3.1882 is used here and the three-way disagreement is recorded rather than resolved. The demolition of the house 'around 1970' is Wikipedia's phrasing and carries no exact date.
stops.campa: In a flat at the head of Leith Walk, Mary Foley delivers a son to Charles Altamont Doyle, a clerk in the Scottish Office who draws and paints considerably better than he holds a post. They name him Arthur Ignatius Conan Doyle. The Doyles are Irish Catholics in a Presbyterian city, genteel in manner and short of money in fact, and the father's drinking is already the household's weather. The house comes down around 1970. A bronze Sherlock Holmes now stands on the ground where it stood, put up to a man who was never born and never died.
suggested_refs: The site of 11 Picardy Place, demolished c. 1970; the Sherlock Holmes statue now standing there

stops.name: St Mary's Roman Catholic Church, Broughton Street: the baptism
stops.date_confidence: The church is attested: Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', names St Mary's as the baptism church. The date 24 May 1859 is not in that article and comes from the dossier alone, so it is reconstruction. The building is named here by the name it carried in 1859, St Mary's Roman Catholic Church; it was raised to cathedral rank only in 1878, and calling the 1859 font a cathedral font would be an anachronism. The pin sits roughly 100 m south of the church.
stops.campa: Two days after the birth the child is carried down Broughton Street and baptised into the faith both sides of the family keep, in what is then a plain Catholic church in a Protestant capital. It holds him about twenty years. Jesuit preparatory school, Jesuit college, a Jesuit year in Austria, and then nothing: by the time he qualifies as a doctor he describes himself as an agnostic and will not accept anything he cannot be shown. What replaces the faith takes another thirty-five years to arrive, and when it does he calls it a new revelation and means the word exactly.
stops.quote: Never will I accept anything which cannot be proved to me. The evils of religion have all come from accepting things which cannot be proved.
stops.quote_source: Memories and Adventures (1924), ch. III, verified verbatim in Project Gutenberg #66991
suggested_refs: St Mary's, Broughton Street, Edinburgh, cathedral from 1878
sources: Arthur Conan Doyle, Memories and Adventures (1924), Project Gutenberg #66991

stops.name: Hodder Place, Stonyhurst: the boy sent south
stops.date_confidence: Attendance and the 1868 year are attested in Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle'; no month or day is given, so the date defaults to 01-01. Hodder Place sits adjacent to Stonyhurst proper and the building coordinate is approximate. That richer relatives paid the fees is standard biography, not independently refetched, and is reconstruction here.
stops.campa: Wealthier relatives on the Doyle side pay to send the nine-year-old into Lancashire, to the Jesuit preparatory school in the valley below Stonyhurst. He goes alone, by train, out of a house where his father is coming apart. At Hodder the discipline is clerical and the homesickness is entirely his own, and he answers it the way he will answer everything: by writing to his mother. He writes to her constantly, and goes on writing to her for the rest of her life. It is the one unbroken line running through a childhood that has otherwise been taken apart and dealt out to whoever will house a boy.
suggested_refs: The Hodder Place preparatory school buildings, Stonyhurst estate

stops.name: Stonyhurst College, Hurst Green: the storyteller and the names
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Stonyhurst College', confirms his attendance and both the Moriarty and Baskerville Hall connections; it does not give exact dates, and the 1870-1875 span comes from the chronology in Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle'. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. That the stories were traded for pastry is standard biographical tradition, not verified in this pass.
stops.campa: He passes up into the senior college for five years of Jesuit rule, harsh discipline, and Lancashire winters. The belief the school exists to instil does not survive them. What does survive is a trade: he finds he can hold a roomful of boys with a serial story told aloud, broken off at the worst possible moment and resumed only on terms. Two names leave with him as well, a schoolfellow called Moriarty, who will lend his surname to the man who kills the detective, and the college hall itself, which becomes Baskerville Hall.
suggested_refs: Stonyhurst College hall, model for Baskerville Hall

stops.name: Stella Matutina, Feldkirch: the year in the Vorarlberg
stops.date_confidence: The year and the fact of attendance are attested in the chronology of Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle'. No dedicated page on Stella Matutina could be fetched in the research pass, so the school's own record is a gap; the dates and attendance are consistent across the biographies the dossier cites. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: A further Jesuit year in the Vorarlberg, at a school where the teaching is in German and the boys come from across Catholic central Europe. He improves the language enough to read it for the remainder of his life and sees, for the first time, a continent that is neither Britain nor Lancashire. The doctrine has loosened past holding by the time the schooling ends. He goes home to Edinburgh in 1876, to a city whose medical school teaches its students to look first and believe afterwards, and matriculates there in the autumn, seventeen years old.
suggested_refs: Stella Matutina, the Jesuit college at Feldkirch, Austria

segments.name: The Medical School and the Method of Joseph Bell

stops.name: Sciennes, Edinburgh: the reassembled household
stops.date_confidence: Source conflict, left open. Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', gives the family address as 3 Sciennes Place; the dossier gives 3 Sciennes Hill Place. These are two distinct adjacent Edinburgh streets and nothing fetched establishes them as one address, so both forms are named and the identification is not asserted. The Liberton Bank House boarding (c. 1866-1868, with the family friend Mary Burton) is reconstruction. Charles Doyle's death at the Crichton Royal on 10 October 1893 comes from a modern psychiatric-history synthesis in the dossier, not independently refetched.
stops.campa: The scattered household reassembles in a rented flat south of the Meadows, at an address the sources give as 3 Sciennes Place and as 3 Sciennes Hill Place and do not reconcile. Arthur has been boarded out during the worst of it, with a family friend at Liberton Bank House on the southern edge of the city. Genteel front rooms; chronic shortage behind them. Charles Altamont Doyle is pensioned off, institutionalised, and dies in 1893 at the Crichton Royal near Dumfries, having filled sketchbooks in the asylum with fairies and grotesques. His son almost never speaks of him in public.
suggested_refs: The asylum sketchbooks of Charles Altamont Doyle
Liberton Bank House, Gilmerton Road, Edinburgh
sources: dossier synthesis of the psychiatric-history literature on Charles Doyle (uncorroborated in this pass)

stops.name: Old College, University of Edinburgh: matriculation and the first sale
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', gives entry to the Edinburgh medical school in 1876 and the anonymous publication of 'The Mystery of Sasassa Valley' in Chambers's Edinburgh Journal on 6 September 1879. The stop is dated to the matriculation year, month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The fee he was paid is not recorded in any fetched source and is not stated here.
stops.campa: He lives at home and takes paid assistantships in the vacations, because the family needs the money more than he needs a holiday. The course is crowded, cheap, and famously hard, and it is the making of him in a way the Jesuit years were not. On 6 September 1879, still a student, he sells a story called 'The Mystery of Sasassa Valley' to Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, anonymously, and from that autumn he never entirely stops writing for money. What the journal paid him for it is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, 6 September 1879, 'The Mystery of Sasassa Valley'

stops.name: Edinburgh Royal Infirmary: outpatient clerk to Joseph Bell
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Joseph Bell', states that Doyle served as Bell's outpatient clerk at the Edinburgh Royal Infirmary and dates their meeting to 1877. The specific diagnostic feats described are the standard illustrations given in the biographical literature rather than a transcript of any one consultation. That Doyle wrote to Bell in 1892 acknowledging the debt is attested in the same source; the letter's text was not fetched, so it is not quoted here.
stops.campa: As outpatient clerk he sits at a desk in the consulting room and calls the patients through. Bell looks at each one before speaking and then tells them their trade, their old regiment, where they have lately travelled, which hand they favour, reading it off boots, hands, gait, and the tan line at a collar. The students are astonished. Bell insists there is nothing in it but observation carried out properly, which is the harder claim. Fifteen years later Doyle writes to him and says it outright: the detective came out of this room, and the method is his teacher's, not his own.
suggested_refs: Doyle's 1892 letter to Joseph Bell acknowledging Holmes's origin

stops.name: Ruyton-XI-Towns, Shropshire: four months unpaid
stops.date_confidence: Attested and corrected: Wikipedia, 'Ruyton-XI-Towns', states that Doyle worked as an unpaid assistant in the village for a Dr Eliot for four months in 1878, living at Cliffe House, and quotes his own 1923 description of the place. The coordinate here is that article's own figure (52 degrees 47 minutes 35 seconds N, 2 degrees 53 minutes 56 seconds W); the research pool carried 52.8156/-2.9432, about 4 km out. The Sheffield and Aston placements are dossier-only, consistently reported but not independently refetched.
stops.campa: Four unpaid months in a Shropshire village, assisting a Dr Eliot and lodging at Cliffe House, learning what a country practice actually consists of: rounds, births, drunks, and the long walk between them. There are other placements in these student years, three weeks at Sheffield and a longer and better-paid stretch at Aston in Birmingham under Dr Reginald Hoare, where he earns enough to matter to the household budget. All of it goes into The Stark Munro Letters twenty years later. Writing in old age, what he remembers about Ruyton is the arithmetic of its name.
stops.quote: not big enough to make one town, far less eleven
stops.quote_source: Memories and Adventures (1923), on Ruyton-XI-Towns, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Ruyton-XI-Towns'
suggested_refs: Cliffe House, Ruyton-XI-Towns
Arthur Conan Doyle, The Stark Munro Letters (1895)

stops.name: Peterhead harbour: signing aboard the whaler Hope
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the chronology of Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', which gives 1880 and the Hope under Captain John Gray; February as the sailing month and Peterhead as home port come from the dossier and standard maritime record, not independently refetched, so the day is defaulted to 01. Doyle's own diary of the voyage was published in 2012 as Dangerous Work and is the primary source for the months at sea.
stops.campa: A fellow student gives up a berth and Doyle takes it: seven months as unqualified ship's surgeon aboard the Arctic whaler Hope, out of Peterhead under Captain John Gray. He is twenty and has not finished his degree, and on a working whaler the surgeon's real function is to be another pair of hands on the ice. He buys a notebook. What he keeps in it, in pen and watercolour, is the only sustained day-by-day record he ever made of anything. The Hope clears the harbour in February for the Greenland grounds.
suggested_refs: Arthur Conan Doyle, Dangerous Work: Diary of an Arctic Adventure (2012), the 1880 logbook
sources: dossier chronology, citing the published 1880 diary

stops.name: The Greenland grounds: seven months on the ice
stops.date_confidence: The voyage is attested in Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle'; the incidents come from Doyle's own diary as published in 2012. The tracklines of the Hope's cruise are not established in any fetched source, so the coordinate is a representative point in the sealing and whaling grounds and carries wide uncertainty. The April date is an ordering device inside the February-to-August voyage, not an attested day.
stops.campa: Months among the seals and the right whales, in an open boat, on the ice, with a lance. He falls through into the water repeatedly and is fished out each time. He treats crushed hands and frostbite, boxes on deck with the steward, joins the hunt rather than watching it, and fills the notebook with drawings of what he has seen killed. The logbook stays in the family, unread outside it, for a hundred and thirty years before anyone prints it. He comes ashore in August, twenty-one years old, and goes back to Edinburgh to finish the degree.
suggested_refs: The illustrated 1880 Arctic logbook, printed 2012 as Dangerous Work

stops.name: Lagos: the fever aboard the SS Mayumba
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the chronology of Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle': the M.B., C.M. taken at Edinburgh in 1881 and the Mayumba voyage to the West African coast in the same year, with a severe fever contracted at Lagos and identified retrospectively as malaria. The retrospective diagnosis is not proven in any source and is flagged as such in the dossier. The month is an ordering device; no day is recorded.
stops.campa: Qualified M.B., C.M. at Edinburgh that summer, he signs on as ship's surgeon aboard a passenger and cargo steamer working the West African coast. The voyage gives him a fire at sea, heavy weather, and at Lagos a fever that nearly kills him and gets called malaria afterwards without anyone ever having proved it. He sweats it out alone in a cabin. He dislikes the coast, dislikes what the ships are carrying and for whom, and comes home certain that whatever he is going to do with his life, it will not be done at sea.
suggested_refs: Arthur Conan Doyle, Memories and Adventures (1924), on the Mayumba voyage
sources: dossier chronology, citing Memories and Adventures

segments.name: Southsea: The Empty Surgery and Sherlock Holmes

stops.name: 1 Bush Villas, Elm Grove: the practice with no patients
stops.date_confidence: Address and date attested: Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', gives the June 1882 opening of the practice at 1 Bush Villas, Elm Grove, Southsea, with very little capital; the M.D. of 1885 on a thesis titled 'An Essay upon the Vasomotor Changes in Tabes Dorsalis'; and the sale of A Study in Scarlet outright to Ward, Lock and Co. for a flat 25 pounds, accepted 20 November 1886 and published in the 1887 Beeton's Christmas Annual. The Plymouth partnership with Dr George Turnavine Budd is dossier-only, standard biography, not refetched. Day of month for the June opening defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He arrives from Plymouth, where a six-week partnership with the volatile Dr George Budd has ended in a quarrel, carrying almost no capital at all. He rents the house, puts up a plate, buys furniture on credit, and waits. Patients come slowly and few. He eats cheaply, keeps no servant, and fills the empty hours with writing, taking an Edinburgh M.D. in 1885 on a thesis about tabes dorsalis to keep the professional side moving. In 1886 he writes A Study in Scarlet in this house and sells it outright to Ward, Lock for twenty-five pounds, all rights, forever.
suggested_refs: Beeton's Christmas Annual, 1887, first printing of A Study in Scarlet
Doyle's M.D. thesis, 'An Essay upon the Vasomotor Changes in Tabes Dorsalis' (1885)

stops.name: Thornton-in-Lonsdale: the marriage to Louisa Hawkins
stops.date_confidence: Upgraded from reconstruction to attested in verification: Wikipedia, 'Thornton in Lonsdale', states that Doyle married his first wife at this church in 1885, held the reception at The Marton Arms, and left for a honeymoon in Ireland, and adds that his mother resided at nearby Masongill from 1882 to 1917. The 6 August 1885 date comes from the chronology in Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle'. The coordinate is that article's own (54 degrees 13 minutes 24 seconds N, 2 degrees 26 minutes 11 seconds W); the research pool carried 54.167/-2.381, about 7.5 km southeast of the village.
stops.campa: He marries Louisa Hawkins at the parish church, in the Yorkshire dale where his mother has been living at Masongill since 1882. He met the bride through her brother, a patient in the Southsea house. The reception is at the Marton Arms and the honeymoon is in Ireland. Touie, as the household calls her, is mild and uncomplaining and in 1893 will be told she has consumption and months to live. She lives thirteen more years, in Switzerland and Egypt and a house built for her lungs, and he nurses her through every one of them while in love with somebody else.
suggested_refs: St Oswald's, Thornton-in-Lonsdale, and the Marton Arms

stops.name: Southsea: the goalkeeper and the Freemason
stops.date_confidence: The Freemasonry is attested: Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', gives initiation at Phoenix Lodge No. 257, Southsea, on 26 January 1887, and dates his interest in psychical research to the mid-1880s. The football is reconstruction: the dossier reports the A. C. Smith pseudonym and the amateur Portsmouth club but flags the club's identity as hard to reconstruct, and the ground's location and dates could not be confirmed in this pass. The coordinate is the dossier's approximate ground and should not be read as a confirmed venue.
stops.campa: The practice leaves him time and he fills it with the town. He keeps goal for an amateur Portsmouth club under the name A. C. Smith, a private enthusiasm quite separate from the professional club founded later and often confused with it. On 26 January 1887 he is initiated into Freemasonry at Phoenix Lodge No. 257, in a town where a young doctor with too few patients is expected to be seen. In the same years, in the same borrowed rooms and drawing rooms, he begins sitting at table-turning experiments with friends, taking notes on what the table does.
suggested_refs: The minute books of Phoenix Lodge No. 257, Southsea

stops.name: London: the Lippincott's dinner
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', attests that The Sign of the Four was commissioned at a London dinner also attended by Oscar Wilde and published in February 1890. The dinner's host J. M. Stoddart, its August 1889 date, and the pairing with the commission of The Picture of Dorian Gray come from the dossier and general literary history and were not independently verified; Oscar Wilde's own journey file stages the Dorian Gray outcome at Tite Street and does not name Doyle. No venue is attested, so the coordinate is a central London placeholder and not a location claim. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: An American editor takes a table in London to commission fiction for a Philadelphia magazine. Doyle is one guest and Oscar Wilde is another, and they are as unlike as English letters can arrange: the Southsea doctor with a failed practice and an outright-sold detective, and the Irishman at the height of his talk. They sit at the same table for one evening. Out of it come two books, printed in the same magazine within months of each other, and one of them makes Sherlock Holmes worth continuing.
suggested_refs: Lippincott's Monthly Magazine, February 1890 (The Sign of the Four) and July 1890 (The Picture of Dorian Gray)

segments.name: The Strand, the Alps, and the Death of Sherlock Holmes

stops.name: 2 Upper Wimpole Street: the consulting room nobody entered
stops.date_confidence: Attested with an unresolved address conflict. Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', gives the 1891 Vienna ophthalmology study, the return to London, and the eye consulting room, but reports the address both as 2 Upper Wimpole Street and as 2 Devonshire Place; the dossier flags the same uncertainty. Both are left standing. 'A Scandal in Bohemia' in the Strand of July 1891, illustrated by Sidney Paget, is separately attested. Month and day for the move unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Fresh from a winter of ophthalmology in Vienna, where the lectures were in German and defeated him, he takes rooms in the specialists' quarter, at an address the sources give as 2 Upper Wimpole Street and as 2 Devonshire Place and do not reconcile, and hangs out a plate as an eye surgeon. By his own account not one patient ever crosses the threshold. So he sits in his own waiting room with a notebook and writes short stories instead, and in July the Strand prints 'A Scandal in Bohemia' with Sidney Paget's drawings, and the queues form at the bookstalls on the day of issue. Within a year he has given up medicine altogether.
suggested_refs: The Strand Magazine, July 1891, 'A Scandal in Bohemia', illustrated by Sidney Paget

stops.name: Davos: skis on the Alpine passes
stops.date_confidence: The residence at Davos for Louisa's tuberculosis in the winter of 1892-93 and Doyle's skiing are attested in the dossier, citing his own Strand article 'An Alpine Pass on Ski'. The dossier itself explicitly flags as overstatement the later claim that Doyle introduced skiing to the Alps; that overstatement is rejected here rather than repeated. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Louisa is diagnosed consumptive in the autumn and the specialists prescribe dry cold air, so the household goes up to the Swiss sanatorium town where the English go to be ill. He fills the days by having Norwegian skis sent out and going up the passes on them at a time when no English visitor in the place has heard of the sport. He writes it up for the Strand as 'An Alpine Pass on Ski'. He did not introduce skiing to the Alps, whatever was later claimed for him and by him, and the claim is worth rejecting plainly rather than repeating. He advertised it.
suggested_refs: Arthur Conan Doyle, 'An Alpine Pass on Ski', Strand Magazine
sources: dossier, citing 'An Alpine Pass on Ski'

stops.name: Reichenbach Falls: a worthy tomb for poor Sherlock
stops.date_confidence: Split evidence. The December 1893 publication of 'The Final Problem' in the Strand is attested (Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle'), as is the coordinate, which matches Wikipedia, 'Reichenbach Falls' exactly (46 degrees 42 minutes 49 seconds N, 8 degrees 10 minutes 59 seconds E). The visit itself is reconstruction: that article gives no date for it and rests the Sir Henry Lunn story on a grandson's family recollection, and the research pool's own date field conceded that the date of the visit is unrecorded. The plaque at the falls dating the fictional struggle to 4 May 1891 is from the same article.
stops.campa: On a Swiss holiday his host walks him up the gorge above Meiringen, where the water comes down through the rock in a series of drops with the spray standing over it. Doyle is tired of Sherlock Holmes, who has taken over a life he had meant to spend writing historical novels, and has already decided to kill him. The falls supply the grave. In December the Strand prints 'The Final Problem' and the detective goes over the lip locked in Moriarty's arms, and a plaque at the place now dates the struggle that never happened to 4 May 1891.
stops.quote: Therefore as a sign of my resolution I determined to end the life of my hero.
stops.quote_source: Memories and Adventures (1924), ch. X, 'The Great Break', verified verbatim in Project Gutenberg #66991
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque at the Reichenbach Falls, Meiringen

stops.name: Cairo and the Nile frontier: the Korosko country
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the dossier chronology, citing Doyle's published Westminster Gazette reporting from the Dongola campaign and The Tragedy of the Korosko (1898). No single fixed itinerary point is given in any fetched source, so the coordinate is Cairo as the general theatre of the winter rather than a place he stood on a stated day. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Another winter cure for Louisa, this one on the Nile, with the Mahdist frontier a few days upriver and Kitchener's reconquest being assembled behind them. Doyle goes further south than the tourist parties usually do, and when the Dongola campaign opens he files for the Westminster Gazette. What he carries home is The Tragedy of the Korosko, a novel about a party of European sightseers taken off a Nile steamer by raiders, written by a man who has been on that steamer and has worked out precisely how thin the arrangement protecting it was.
suggested_refs: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Tragedy of the Korosko (1898); his Westminster Gazette dispatches from the Dongola campaign
sources: dossier chronology, citing the published dispatches and the novel

stops.name: Undershaw, Hindhead: the house Holmes paid for
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Undershaw', confirms the house, its 1897 construction by the architect Joseph Henry Ball, and the family's residence from 1897 to 1907, and supplies this coordinate. Doyle's meeting with Jean Leckie in 1897 is attested in Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle'; the specific date of 15 March 1897 is dossier-only. The Allahakbarries membership is attested from the atlas's own J. M. Barrie file, but the club had no fixed ground and played around London and Surrey, so it is attached here to the Surrey years and not to this pin. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Sherlock Holmes pays for the house: a large red-brick place on a Surrey hillside chosen for dry air, its stained glass displaying the arms of the family's claimed descent from the Percys of Northumberland. Louisa is installed in it to breathe. He writes The Hound of the Baskervilles here, which means bringing the dead detective back for one story set before the falls. Through these same years he turns out on Surrey grass for J. M. Barrie's Allahakbarries, an amateur eleven of novelists whose competence at cricket was mostly notional. And in March 1897 he has met Jean Leckie.
suggested_refs: Undershaw, Hindhead, built 1897 by Joseph Henry Ball; from 2016 the Stepping Stones School

segments.name: The Public Man: the War, the Knighthood, the Wronged

stops.name: Bloemfontein: the Langman Field Hospital
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', confirms the Langman Field Hospital at Bloemfontein, his service there as a volunteer physician, and the March to June 1900 span. The coordinate is Bloemfontein city centre; the hospital site itself was not separately located in the research pass. That he was rejected for a combat commission is in the same chronology. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Forty years old and refused for a fighting commission, he goes out as a volunteer senior physician with a privately funded field hospital in a captured town. Afterwards he writes a pamphlet defending British conduct in the war, and will maintain ever after that the knighthood came for the pamphlet and not for Sherlock Holmes. That is afterwards. Here, enteric fever moves through the British army faster than any Boer commando and kills more men than the shooting does, and he works among them for three months in conditions no hospital in England would have been permitted to keep.
suggested_refs: Arthur Conan Doyle, The War in South Africa: Its Cause and Conduct (1902)

stops.name: Edinburgh Central: the seat he did not win
stops.date_confidence: Attested and corrected in verification: Wikipedia, 'Edinburgh Central (UK Parliament constituency)', gives the 1900 result as George Mackenzie Brown (Liberal) 3,028 votes, 55.2 per cent, against Arthur Conan Doyle (Liberal Unionist) 2,459, 44.8 per cent, a majority of 569, on a turnout of 5,487 of 7,630 electors, 71.9 per cent. The research pool named the winner 'C. M. Brown', which is wrong; the vote totals it carried are confirmed. The coordinate is the corpus-standard Edinburgh pin, reused from J. M. Barrie's file. Day of the poll defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Home from South Africa with a reputation and no political machinery whatever, he stands for his native city as a Liberal Unionist, in an election fought on the war he has just come back from. Edinburgh made him a doctor and gave him the method he has built a career on, and 7,630 men on its register are entitled to vote. 5,487 of them do. The Liberal George Mackenzie Brown takes the seat with 3,028 votes, 55.2 per cent, against his 2,459, a majority of 569 on a turnout of just under seventy-two per cent.
suggested_refs: The 1900 Edinburgh Central poll book

stops.name: Buckingham Palace: the accolade, and Holmes brought back
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', gives the accolade of Knight Bachelor from Edward VII at Buckingham Palace on 24 October 1902, the Knight of Grace of the Order of St John in 1903, and 'The Adventure of the Empty House' in 1903, driven partly by large American publisher offers. The belief that the honour rewarded his South African writing and hospital service rather than the fiction is his own, as recorded in the same source.
stops.campa: Edward VII gives him the accolade of Knight Bachelor. He is convinced the honour is for the war pamphlet and the hospital tents at Bloemfontein and not for the detective, and he says so; the public assumes the opposite and always will. The next year he is made a Knight of Grace of the Order of St John. The next year, too, with American publishers offering sums that no argument about literary dignity survives, 'The Adventure of the Empty House' explains that Holmes never fell at all, and the man he had drowned nine years earlier walks back into Baker Street through a locked door.
suggested_refs: The Strand Magazine, 1903, 'The Adventure of the Empty House'

stops.name: Great Wyrley, Staffordshire: the fields walked at night
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'George Edalji', confirms that Doyle went to the crime scenes and interviewed participants, and dates his direct involvement, his meeting with Edalji, and his approach to Chief Constable Anson to January 1907. This contradicts the research pool's geography lens, which dated the involvement to 1906; the January 1907 date is used here and the contradiction is recorded. Doyle first read Edalji's own statement in The Umpire in late 1906, per Memories and Adventures. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Livestock has been ripped open in the fields around this Staffordshire mining village, and George Edalji, a solicitor and the son of a Parsi vicar, has served three years of penal servitude for it. Doyle reads the man's own account of the case in an obscure paper called The Umpire and takes it up. He walks the lanes between the vicarage and the fields himself, in the dark and the mud, timing the distances, examining the coat and the razors and the ground, and concludes in public that the police built their case backwards from the family they had already selected.
stops.quote: As I read, the unmistakable accent of truth forced itself upon my attention and I realized that I was in the presence of an appalling tragedy, and that I was called upon to do what I could to set it right.
stops.quote_source: Memories and Adventures (1924), ch. XXI, 'The Years Between the Wars', verified verbatim in Project Gutenberg #66991
suggested_refs: The Umpire, late 1906, George Edalji's own statement of his case

stops.name: A London hotel: reading Edalji across the lobby
stops.date_confidence: Venue unattested and date corrected. Wikipedia, 'George Edalji', names only 'a hotel' and supplies no venue, so the research pool's 'Grand Hotel lobby' and this coordinate are a central London placeholder, not a location claim. The same article dates the meeting to January 1907, against the pool's geography lens, which had 1906; the article also records that Chief Constable Anson turned hostile two days after their meeting, that the Home Office inquiry produced a pardon in May 1907 for the maiming conviction, that compensation was refused on the ground that Edalji had written certain anonymous letters, and that he was reinstated to the solicitors' roll later that year. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He arranges to meet the convicted man in a hotel and arrives early on purpose. Instead of going over he watches him read a newspaper, holding it sideways and close to his face at an angle nobody with ordinary sight would use. Doyle has his answer before a word passes: severe myopia, a man who could not have crossed those fields in the dark, found a pony, and cut it. It is Joseph Bell's method, worked in a hotel lounge on a living man. The pardon comes in May, for the maiming and not for the anonymous letters the Home Office holds he wrote, and on that ground it refuses him compensation. Who wrote the letters the inquiry never establishes.
suggested_refs: The Home Office committee report of May 1907 on the Edalji conviction

stops.name: Windlesham, Crowborough: the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: Dates attested in the chronology of Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle': Louisa's death on 4 July 1906 after long tubercular illness, the meeting with Jean Leckie in 1897, the marriage in September 1907, and Windlesham as the house he kept until his death. The characterisation of the courtship as scrupulously unconsummated is standard biography and reconstruction, not documented in any fetched source. The coordinate approximates Crowborough; no dedicated page for the house could be fetched (404). Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Louisa dies in July 1906, thirteen years after being given months. Fourteen months later he marries Jean Leckie, whom he has loved since 1897 and, by every account the family left behind, never touched and never hid in the ten years he spent nursing his wife. No document fetched for this file proves the abstinence; it is what the biographies say and what the family said. They buy a house on the Sussex ridge above Crowborough and he lives in it for twenty-three years, the rest of his life. Whether Louisa knew is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Windlesham Manor, Crowborough, East Sussex

stops.name: White City Stadium: Dorando Pietri carried over the line
stops.date_confidence: Attested and corrected. Wikipedia, 'White City Stadium' and 'Dorando Pietri' confirm the date, the Daily Mail commission, Pietri's collapse and four further falls, the disqualification on the American protest, and Doyle's line about the Italian's performance. Two corrections to the research pool: the subscription Doyle proposed was to raise money for Pietri's bakery and reached 300 pounds, not for a silver cup, which was Queen Alexandra's separate consolation gift; and the 5 pounds Doyle put in himself is attested, not weakly sourced as the pool's note claimed.
stops.campa: Commissioned by the Daily Mail to report the Olympic marathon, he watches from the press seats as Dorando Pietri comes into the stadium first, turns the wrong way, and goes down. Officials pick him up. He falls four more times in the last stretch and is helped over the line, and the Americans protest, and he is disqualified. Doyle's account of it makes the Italian a hero across Britain within a day. He proposes a public subscription for the man's bakery and puts in the first five pounds himself; it reaches three hundred.
stops.quote: The Italian's great performance can never be effaced from our record of sport.
stops.quote_source: Arthur Conan Doyle, Daily Mail report of the 1908 Olympic marathon, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Dorando Pietri'
suggested_refs: The Daily Mail marathon report, 25 July 1908; the Pietri subscription fund

stops.name: West Princes Street, Glasgow: the case of Oscar Slater
stops.date_confidence: Attested with two flags. Wikipedia, 'Oscar Slater', gives the December 1908 murder of Marion Gilchrist, aged 83, beaten to death in a robbery in West Princes Street, Glasgow, and dates Doyle's The Case of Oscar Slater to 1912. That article does not supply a house number, so the research pool's '49' is dossier-only; the address traditionally given in the case literature is 15 Queen's Terrace, West Princes Street. The coordinate sits roughly 350 m east of West Princes Street and is carried forward unresolved. The 1928 quashing after nearly nineteen years, and the compensation, are dossier-only, widely corroborated but not refetched. Stop dated to the campaign's opening year; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: An eighty-three-year-old woman named Marion Gilchrist is beaten to death in her flat in December 1908, and a German Jewish gambler named Oscar Slater is convicted on identification evidence that will not carry the weight put on it, sentenced to hang, and reprieved into penal servitude two days before the rope. Doyle takes the printed record apart in 1912 in The Case of Oscar Slater and then does not let go of it for sixteen years, against the Scottish legal establishment, the police, and eventually Slater himself, who quarrelled with him about the costs. The conviction is quashed in July 1928.
stops.quote: It is a dreadful blot upon the administration of justice in Scotland, and such judicial crimes are not, I am convinced, done with impunity even to the most humble.
stops.quote_source: Memories and Adventures (1924), ch. XXI, written while Slater was still imprisoned; verified verbatim in Project Gutenberg #66991
suggested_refs: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Case of Oscar Slater (1912)

stops.name: Wellington House, Buckingham Gate: twenty-five writers sworn to silence
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Wellington House', confirms 2 September 1914, Charles Masterman, twenty-five leading British authors including Doyle, Hardy, Bennett, Wells and Chesterton, Kipling invited but unable to attend, and the secrecy holding until 1935. Coordinate corrected: that article locates the building at the corner of Petty France, formerly York Street, and Buckingham Gate, which is nearer 51.4996/-0.1370 than the research pool's 51.4989/-0.1417, about 350 m west of the named corner.
stops.campa: Twenty-five of the best-known writers in Britain are called in secret to a building at the corner of Petty France and Buckingham Gate. Hardy is there, and Wells, and Bennett, and Chesterton, and Doyle; Kipling is invited and cannot come. Charles Masterman explains what the government wants of them and they agree to supply it, and they agree to say nothing whatever about the meeting. The pledge holds for twenty-one years. Doyle spends the war writing a six-volume history of the British campaign in France and Flanders with the co-operation of the generals whose battles he is describing.
suggested_refs: The War Propaganda Bureau at Wellington House, Buckingham Gate

stops.name: The Western Front: the eminent visitor
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the dossier chronology, citing Doyle's own published A Visit to Three Fronts (1916) and The British Campaign in France and Flanders. No fixed itinerary is specified in any fetched source, so the coordinate is a representative point in the Somme sector. Kingsley Conan Doyle's birth on 15 November 1892 and his death in 1918 are attested in Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', and in The Wanderings of a Spiritualist; the Somme wound is dossier detail. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Given passes and staff transport, he tours the line as a distinguished visitor and watches from observation posts the war his son is fighting in. He is fifty-seven and has been refused, again, for anything nearer the fighting than this. Out of the tour comes A Visit to Three Fronts, and he goes on with the six volumes, patriotic, meticulously sourced, written from inside the official machinery rather than at any distance from it. His son Kingsley is wounded on the Somme, survives the wound, and dies in 1918, at twenty-five, of illness.
suggested_refs: Arthur Conan Doyle, A Visit to Three Fronts (1916) and The British Campaign in France and Flanders, 6 vols.
sources: dossier chronology, citing the published works

stops.name: London: the Congo book and the petition for Casement
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the chronology of Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle': The Crime of the Congo (1909) attacking forced-labour atrocities under Leopold II and lending his celebrity to the Congo Reform Association; and his appeal for clemency for Roger Casement, convicted of treason after seeking German aid for Irish independence, refused. The execution date of 3 August 1916 is corroborated by the dossier and was not independently refetched. That Doyle knew Casement personally is standard biography and reconstruction. The coordinate is a central London placeholder, no venue being attested for the petition.
stops.campa: In 1909 he writes The Crime of the Congo, an account of the forced-labour terror in Leopold's Free State, and lends his name and his sales to the reform campaign, whose whole evidentiary case rests on Roger Casement's consular reporting. Seven years later Casement is condemned for treason, having gone to Germany to seek arms for a rising in Ireland. Doyle signs and organises a clemency petition and argues in it that the man who documented the Congo and the Putumayo had been driven out of his judgement by what he had been sent to look at. Casement is hanged on 3 August 1916.
suggested_refs: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Crime of the Congo (1909); the 1916 Casement clemency petition

stops.name: The Royal Albert Hall: the lecture and the empty chair
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The dossier reports both the 1919 Spiritualist lectures at the Royal Albert Hall and the memorial gathering of 13 July 1930 with a chair left empty on the platform, citing the standard Spiritualist-movement record; neither was independently refetched in this pass, and the empty-chair episode is widely and consistently reported rather than documented from a primary account. The stop is dated to the lecture years, which are Doyle's own; the 1930 memorial is recorded inside the campa as a posthumous fact and is not staged as a scene he attended. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: He lectures here in the missionary years, a large heavy man with a Scottish voice and a slide projector, holding several thousand people on the survival of the personality after bodily death. He is the most credible witness the movement has ever had and he knows exactly what his credibility is worth to it. Six days after his death, on 13 July 1930, the Spiritualists fill this same hall for a memorial meeting and leave a chair empty on the platform beside Jean and the children, on the stated understanding that it will not be empty. A medium told the audience she could see him in it.
suggested_refs: The Royal Albert Hall memorial meeting of 13 July 1930
sources: dossier, Death/Burial and 1919-1924 sections (not independently refetched)

stops.name: Devonshire: the sitting with Evan Powell
stops.date_confidence: The sitting is attested in Doyle's own words, verified verbatim in The Wanderings of a Spiritualist (1921), ch. I, Project Gutenberg #39718: he describes a seance with the medium Evan Powell in Devonshire before departing on the lecture tour, and reports speaking with his dead son Kingsley. No venue is named in the text, so the coordinate is a county placeholder for Devon and not a location claim. The month is inferred from the tour's departure and is an ordering device; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Kingsley has been dead two years. Doyle has announced publicly that the dead speak, that the evidence for it is as good as evidence gets, and that he intends to spend whatever is left of his life and his money saying so. Before sailing for Australia he sits in a darkened room in Devonshire with the medium Evan Powell. He writes the account himself, in the first chapter of a travel book, in the same flat professional voice he used for the fever wards at Bloemfontein and the lanes at Great Wyrley. He has spoken with his son. His son has blessed the mission.
stops.quote: I had the joy of a few last words with my arisen son, who blessed me on my mission and assured me that I would indeed bring solace to bruised hearts.
stops.quote_source: The Wanderings of a Spiritualist (1921), ch. I, verified verbatim in Project Gutenberg #39718
suggested_refs: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Wanderings of a Spiritualist (1921)

stops.name: Sydney: the world mission
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the dossier chronology, citing Doyle's own The Wanderings of a Spiritualist (1921) for the Australian and New Zealand tour of 1920-21 with Jean and the children. No single venue was independently confirmed in this pass, so the coordinate is a representative point for the Australian leg. Month is an ordering device inside the tour; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The mission takes him and Jean and the three young children around the world: Australia first, then New Zealand, full halls, spirit photographs thrown up on a screen, a knight of the realm telling a paying audience that he has spoken with his dead boy. He is sixty-one and among the most famous writers alive, and he is spending the fame on purpose. The Australian press is largely hostile and the halls are largely full, which is the pattern everywhere he goes for the next four years.
suggested_refs: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Wanderings of a Spiritualist (1921), the Australasian tour
sources: dossier chronology, citing The Wanderings of a Spiritualist

stops.name: London: 'Fairies Photographed' in the Strand
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Cottingley Fairies', confirms the 1917 photographs by Elsie Wright and Frances Griffiths, that all direct contact with the Wright family was handled by Edward Gardner on Doyle's behalf, that Doyle did not visit Cottingley himself, the December 1920 Strand article and its rapid sell-out, The Coming of the Fairies (1922), the 1983 confession in The Unexplained, the cardboard cut-outs copied from Claude Shepperson's illustrations in Princess Mary's Gift Book, the hatpins, and Frances's insistence that the fifth photograph was genuine. The stop is deliberately placed in London and not at Cottingley beck, because Doyle never went there: the beck is cited as a reference, not staged as a scene. No venue for the Strand offices is attested, so the coordinate is a central London placeholder. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Two girls in a Yorkshire village photographed themselves among fairies in 1917 and the plates have reached him through a theosophist named Edward Gardner, who handles every contact with the family. Doyle never goes north. He examines the prints, has them tested, is told by several photographic men that they prove nothing either way, and publishes regardless. The Christmas Strand sells out in days and The Coming of the Fairies follows in 1922. The girls confessed in 1983: cardboard cut-outs traced from a children's gift book and propped on hatpins, thrown into the beck afterwards. Frances maintained to the end that one of the five was real.
suggested_refs: The beck at the foot of the Wright garden, Cottingley, West Yorkshire (53.8295, -1.8308), where the photographs were taken
The Cottingley cameras, plates and prints, National Science and Media Museum, Bradford
Arthur Conan Doyle, The Coming of the Fairies (1922)

stops.name: The Ambassador Hotel, Atlantic City: his wife's hand, and the end of a friendship
stops.date_confidence: Date contradiction, unresolved and inherited. Wikipedia, 'Ambassador Hotel (Atlantic City)', dates the Doyle-Houdini meeting and Lady Doyle's automatic-writing session there to 18 June 1922 and is followed here; Houdini's own printed account in A Magician Among the Spirits gives 17 June, and Harry Houdini's journey file in this corpus uses 17 June accordingly. PBS American Experience independently confirms the fifteen sheets of automatic writing and Houdini's objection that his mother had barely uttered a word of English while alive. Two details in the research pool do not survive verification and are omitted: the cross heading the pages appears in neither fetched source, and Cecilia Weiss's birthday is usually given as 16 June, so it did not fall on the day of the sitting. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from harry_houdini.journey.json (the Ambassador stood at 2831 Boardwalk, now the Tropicana).
stops.campa: He has come to America to lecture on survival after death and has brought Harry Houdini, whom he likes enormously and does not understand at all, down to the shore for a few days. In the suite, Jean takes up a pencil, prays, and begins to write, and Doyle watches his wife's hand fill fifteen sheets in the voice of the escapologist's dead mother. He is entirely satisfied. What he believes he has seen is a gift handed to a bereaved friend by the friend's own mother. Houdini sits there and says nothing at the time. The friendship does not survive what he says six months later.
suggested_refs: The fifteen automatic-writing sheets of June 1922, reproduced by Houdini in A Magician Among the Spirits (1924), ch. IX
sources: PBS American Experience, 'Houdini and Conan Doyle'

stops.name: Paris: honorary president of the Spiritualist congress

stops.campa: He presides over the congress as honorary president, delegates from across Europe in front of him, speaking now as the head of a movement rather than as its most distinguished convert. In 1926 he brings out two volumes of The History of Spiritualism, writing the movement's history as a participant in it. By this point he is also running a psychic bookshop, library and lecture room in Victoria Street out of his own pocket, covering the rent himself year after year on a business that never turns a profit and was never meant to. The earnings of Sherlock Holmes go into it.

segments.name: The Last Year and the Grave in the New Forest

stops.name: Bignell Wood, near Minstead: the house burns
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The dossier's 1929-1930 section gives the fire of 15 August 1929 at the family's New Forest property and cites surviving family photographs of furniture carried onto the lawn; it was not independently refetched. The coordinate approximates the Minstead area and the exact house site was not pinpointed in this pass. The angina and heart failure of the last year are attested in Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle'.
stops.campa: Fire badly damages the house the family keeps in the New Forest, and photographs survive of the household carrying furniture out onto the lawn while the flames take the roof. The decade behind him has gone on the mission: lecture tours around the world, a son buried, premises and pamphlets and hired halls paid for out of the detective's earnings. The land here is a few miles from a churchyard he has never particularly thought about, in which he will lie for rather longer than he lived. He is seventy, and the angina that will kill him inside the year has already begun.
suggested_refs: The family photographs of the Bignell Wood fire, 15 August 1929

stops.name: The Home Office, Whitehall: the last deputation
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the dossier's 1929-1930 section, citing the standard biographical chronology: a meeting with Home Secretary J. R. Clynes on 1 July 1930, six days before Doyle's death, to argue for reform of the old witchcraft and vagrancy statutes used against mediums. Not independently refetched in this pass, but consistently reported. That he was visibly ill is from the same source.
stops.campa: Visibly dying, he comes up to London one last time at the head of a deputation to the Home Secretary, to argue for repeal of the old witchcraft and vagrancy statutes under which mediums are still prosecuted as rogues and vagabonds. He can barely get from the car to the room. He makes the argument anyway, and it is the same argument he made for George Edalji and for Oscar Slater: that the law is being applied to a class of people about whom the courts have already made up their minds. Six days later he is dead.
suggested_refs: The Witchcraft Act 1735 and the Vagrancy Act 1824, the statutes under which mediums were prosecuted

stops.name: Windlesham, Crowborough: heart failure at dawn
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', gives death at Windlesham, Crowborough, on 7 July 1930, aged 71, of heart failure after recurrent angina, and records the family account of his last words to Jean. The last words rest on family testimony alone, with no independent transcript, and the dossier flags them explicitly as intimate rather than verifiable testimony; they are given here as a quote with that provenance stated and are reconstruction, not attestation.
stops.campa: He collapses in the house clutching his chest and dies near dawn on the seventh of July, seventy-one years old, of a heart that has been failing for a year. For fourteen years he has told anyone who would listen that death is a door and not a wall, and he has staked a knighthood, a fortune, and one of the largest literary reputations in the English-speaking world on saying so in public. Whether he was frightened at the end is not recorded by anybody. What the family recorded was three words spoken to his wife, and the family are the only witnesses there have ever been.
stops.quote_source: Doyle's last words to Jean Conan Doyle, family testimony only, recorded in Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', with no independent witness
suggested_refs: Windlesham Manor, Crowborough; the statue of Doyle at Crowborough Cross

stops.name: The rose garden at Windlesham: the burial without a church
stops.date_confidence: Date, place and open-air rose-garden setting attested in Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle'. The claim that he was buried standing upright is reconstruction and should not be tagged otherwise: it appears unsourced in Wikipedia, 'Minstead' ('originally buried in a vertical position in Crowborough') and Wikipedia, 'Crowborough' ('initially buried vertically in the grounds of the manor'), which is two Wikipedia pages repeating each other rather than independent attestation. Coordinate conflict flagged and resolved by consistency: the research pool's afterlife lens gave 51.0537/0.1608 for the same house that its geography lens twice gave as 51.0553/0.1547; the latter is used throughout this file.
stops.campa: Four days later he is buried in the rose garden of his own house, in the open air and without a church service. The faith he died in had no consecrated ground to give him and the one he was baptised into he had left at twenty. Jean and the children stand at the graveside, and so do the Spiritualists, who did not regard the occasion as a funeral at all on the grounds that nothing had happened except a change of address. Two later encyclopaedia articles say he was put into the ground standing upright. Neither cites anything for it.
suggested_refs: The Windlesham rose garden grave, 1930-1955

stops.name: All Saints, Minstead: the grave under the tree
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to year and place, with an unresolved conflict about who lies there. Wikipedia, 'Minstead', gives the 1955 reinterment in the churchyard, the plot under a tree on the south side, and this coordinate (50 degrees 54 minutes 10 seconds N, 1 degrees 36 minutes 35 seconds W); the research pool's afterlife lens carried 50.8847/-1.6591, about 4.5 km out in the forest, contradicting its own geography lens. Three readings of the other occupant stand in the sources and are not reconciled here: the pool says Jean Leckie, who died in 1940; Wikipedia, 'Crowborough', says he was 'later interred with his first wife at Minstead'; Wikipedia, 'Minstead', says he was re-interred by the family of his deceased first wife and names the plot's other occupant as 'his daughter Jean Conan Doyle'. No month or day is given for 1955, so the date defaults to 01-01. The inscription wording comes from Wikipedia, 'Arthur Conan Doyle', and from the dossier, not from the Minstead article, which carries no inscription text.
stops.campa: Twenty-five years after his death the family moves the remains into the New Forest churchyard, a few miles from the burnt house, and lays them under a tree on the south side of the ground. The stone reads: Steel true, blade straight, Arthur Conan Doyle, Knight, Patriot, physician and man of letters. Who lies with him is not agreed. One account says his second wife Jean, another says his first wife Louisa, a third names his daughter, and the village record supplies no month or day for the removal either. He wrote sixty stories about a man who could have settled it in an afternoon.
suggested_refs: The Doyle grave, All Saints churchyard, Minstead, Hampshire
